q-69726:
To find $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3}),$ we need to find the number that is located in row $5$ and position $3$ of Pascal's triangle. 

**Important**: When counting the rows and positions in Pascal's triangle, we always start counting from zero! Remember:

- The top row of Pascal's triangle is row $0.$

- The first position of each row (the one of the left) is position number $0.$

The location of $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})$ in Pascal's triangle is highlighted below.

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{0}{0}) \\  &  &  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{1}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{1}{1}) \\  &  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{2}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{2}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{2}{2}) \\  &  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{3}{3}) \\  &  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{4}) \\  &  &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{2}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4}) &  & (\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5}) \\  &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})$ is the sum of the two closest numbers located in the previous row. So,

$$
(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{3})=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2})+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{3})
$$

Therefore, the missing expression is $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}).$

q-69994:
The binomial coefficient $(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{r})$ is given by the formula

$$
(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{r})=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!}.
$$

In this case, we have $n=4$ and $r=2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}) & =\frac{4!}{(4-2)!\cdot 2!} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3\cdot 2!}{2!\cdot 2!} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3\cdot \cancel{2!}}{2\cdot \cancel{2!}} \\  & =\frac{12}{2} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-88006:
First, we isolate the logarithm:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)+4 & \ge 0 \\ \frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & \ge -4 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2) & \ge -6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ We get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-2)} & \ge {e}^{-6} \\ x-2 & \ge {e}^{-6} \\ x & \ge {e}^{-6}+2 \\ x & \ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithm, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
x-2>0\,⇒\,x>2
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domain of the logarithm is $x>2,$ which can be expressed as $(2,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithm, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty )\cap (2,\infty )=[\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x\ge \frac{1+2{e}^{6}}{{e}^{6}}.$

q-88037:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)-2} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)}\cdot {e}^{-2} & \ge {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)} \\ (x-1){e}^{-2} & \ge 5x \\ x-1 & \ge 5{e}^{2}x \\ -1 & \ge (5{e}^{2}-1)x \\ -\frac{1}{5{e}^{2}-1} & \ge x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >1 \\ 5x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >0\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\le -\frac{1}{5{e}^{2}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{5{e}^{2}-1}].$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>1$ and $x>0,$ which can be expressed as $(1,\infty )$ and $(0,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,-\frac{1}{5{e}^{2}-1}]\cap (1,\infty )\cap (0,\infty )=∅
$$

The intersection is empty. Therefore, there is no solution.

q-114551:
We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=9{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int 9{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=3{x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 9{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)(3{x}^{3})-\int \frac{3{x}^{3}}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)-3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{x}^{3}+C \\  & ={x}^{3}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x-1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an integral constant.

q-114679:
First, we write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\text{d}x={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}x.
$$

We will solve this problem using integration by parts. We start by defining $u$ and ${v}^{′},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=\frac{1}{x} \\ {v}^{′}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int 1\cdot \,dx=x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{log}_{3}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\cdot 1\cdot \,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[uv{|}_{1/2}^{1}-{\int }_{1/2}^{1}v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x){|}_{1/2}^{1}-{\int }_{1/2}^{1}x(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot 1)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\cdot \frac{1}{2})-{\int }_{1/2}^{1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡1-x{|}_{1/2}^{1}\,] \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-0-(1-\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}] \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-115431:
First, we move all the terms to the left side of the inequality and factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x\cdot {5}^{x+6}-{5}^{x+6} & <8\cdot {5}^{x+6} \\ 3x\cdot {5}^{x+6}-{5}^{x+6}-8\cdot {5}^{x+6} & <0 \\ (3x-1-8){5}^{x+6} & <0 \\ (3x-9){5}^{x+6} & <0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we divide both sides by ${5}^{x+6}$ and solve the resulting inequality using familiar techniques:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-9 & <0 \\ 3x & <9 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to the inequality above is $x<3.$

q-40368:
First, we define the function $f(x)$ as

$$
f(x)=({x}^{2}+3)(x+3)(x-3).
$$

So we're now solving the inequality $f(x)\ge 0.$

The solutions to the equation $f(x)=0$ are $x=-3$ and $x=3.$ These roots divide the number line into $3$ subintervals:

$$
(-\infty ,-3),\,(-3,3),\,(3,\infty )
$$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-3)$ | $(-3,3)$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}+3$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x+3$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-3$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $f(x)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Finally, to solve the inequality $f(x)\ge 0,$ we look at the bottom row to determine where $f(x)$ is positive.

From the table, we see that $f(x)$ is positive on the intervals $(-\infty ,-3)$ and $(3,\infty ).$

Therefore, remembering that the roots are also solutions, we conclude that $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [3,\infty ).$

q-115673:
First, we find the constant $B.$ Multiplying both sides of the given equality by $(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-5x-27 & =(2x+B)(x+1)-({x}^{2}+20).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-5(0)-27 & =(2(0)+B)(0+1)-({0}^{2}+20) \\ -27 & =B-20 \\ B & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-5x-27}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x-7}{{x}^{2}+20}-\frac{1}{x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x-7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution ${x}^{2}+20=u.$ Then, $2x\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u,$ and we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+20).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+20}\,\text{d}x & =7\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+(2\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{5}}) \\  & =\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{10}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-5x-27}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+20)}\,\text{d}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+20)-\frac{7\sqrt{5}}{10}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{5}x}{10})-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-83161:
First, we find the constant $A.$ Multiplying both sides of the given equality by $({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+x+3 & =(Ax+1)(x-1)+{x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=2$  into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{2}+2+3 & =(A(2)+1)(2-1)+{2}^{2}+4 \\ 9 & =2A+1+8 \\ 9 & =2A+9 \\ A & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{0x+1}{{x}^{2}+4}+\frac{1}{x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+x+3}{({x}^{2}+4)(x-1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-115693:
The quadratic factor ${x}^{2}+3$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)} & =\frac{Ax+B}{{x}^{2}+3}+\frac{C}{x+4}\end{aligned}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $({x}^{2}+3)(x+4),$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+5x-9 & =(Ax+B)(x+4)+C({x}^{2}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=2,B=-3,$ and $C=1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)} & =\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}+3}+\frac{1}{x+4}\end{aligned}
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}+3}+\frac{1}{x+4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+3.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{u}\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+3| \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\begin{aligned}3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x & =3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}+5x-9}{({x}^{2}+3)(x+4)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{x+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3)-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{3})+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+4|+K\end{aligned}
$$

q-49919:
The quadratic factor ${x}^{2}+1$ is irreducible, so we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-1)({x}^{2}+1),$ and we get

$$
2=A({x}^{2}+1)+(Bx+C)(x-1).
$$

Solving for the unknown constants using the usual methods, we get $A=1,B=-1,$ and $C=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}=\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{-x-1}{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

We now integrate this function term by term, adding the constant of integration at the very end.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-1}+\frac{-x-1}{{x}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

For the first integral, we have

$$
\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|.
$$

For the second integral, we use the substitution $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{u})\frac{\text{d}u}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{2}+1| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, for the third integral, we use the fact that $\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{a}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{a}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{a}),$ which results in

$$
\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.
$$

So, we get the following result:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+K\end{aligned}
$$

q-3617:
Notice that the quadratic factor in the denominator has a discriminant that is not a perfect square:

$$
D={4}^{2}-4(1)(-1)=20
$$

We have that $\sqrt{20}$ is not a rational number, which implies that the quadratic factor doesn't factor over the rational numbers.

So, we proceed with the following partial fraction decomposition:

$$
\frac{3{x}^{2}+9x-4}{(x-1)({x}^{2}+4x-1)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{Bx+C}{{x}^{2}+4x-1}
$$
